title: Hurricane Nolo Takes a Sharp Turn Toward Hawaii
summary: Have you ever watched a storm change its mind? Hurricane Nolo did exactly that. Earlier this week, it was heading west across the open ocean. Then it took a sudden right turn — straight toward Hawaii's Big Island. As of Friday, Nolo had winds of 105 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane. But here's the weird part: it was moving at only 5 mph. That's slower than a person riding a bike! Slow storms are dangerous because they dump rain in one place for a long time. Forecasters say some areas could get more than 2 feet of rain, with 10 to 25 inches more widely. That's like pouring a bathtub of water on every square foot of ground. The National Hurricane Center warned of "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides." The Big Island is under a hurricane watch, and Maui is under a tropical storm watch. Nolo isn't expected to make landfall, but it could strengthen to a Category 4 with 140 mph winds. Hawaii has already been hit by four major disasters this year, damaging about 1,290 homes. Governor Josh Green said recovery could cost $1 billion. "The time to finish preparations is now," the NHC said.
why_it_matters: Learning how slow storms cause flooding helps kids understand why families are told to prepare early — and why weather warnings at home are worth paying attention to.

background_read: Hawaii is a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean and the 50th state of the United States.
The National Hurricane Center is the U.S. government team that watches big storms and warns people where they might hit.

Storms like Nolo get their power from warm ocean water and can suddenly change direction when winds push them. Hawaii is not hit by hurricanes very often, but in 1992 Hurricane Iniki badly damaged the island of Kauai.
Article_Structure: WHO: Hurricane Nolo, forecasters at the National Hurricane Center, and Hawaii Governor Josh Green.
WHAT: Nolo suddenly turned toward Hawaii as a Category 2 storm with 105 mph winds, crawling along at only 5 mph and threatening catastrophic flooding and mudslides.
WHERE: The Big Island, which is under a hurricane watch, and Maui, which is under a tropical storm watch.
WHY: Slow storms can pour huge amounts of rain on one spot, and Hawaii has already been hit by four major disasters this year that damaged about 1,290 homes.

perspectives.description: Forecasters and officials say there is still time to prepare, and the watches are meant to give people a head start on buying supplies and making plans.
People in Hawaii have already dealt with four disasters this year, and families still fixing damaged homes may feel they cannot handle more rain and mudslides.
Hurricanes often wobble and change direction, and slow-moving ones are especially hard to predict, so experts say people should keep checking for updates.
